questions.q: A brick-maker leases a riverside plot. She lists her inputs: clay soil from the plot, water from the river, wooden moulds, eight labourers and a loan from a bank. Which pair does the chapter count as 'land'?
questions.a: The clay soil and the river water
o: The clay soil and the river water
The wooden moulds and the river water
The clay soil and the labourers
The bank loan and the wooden moulds

questions.q: Two tea cafes stand on the same road. Café P bought its plot outright. Café Q pays a monthly rent for its plot. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Both use land as a factor, one by purchase and the other by paying rent for a period
o: Both use land as a factor, one by purchase and the other by paying rent for a period
Only Café P uses land, as a business has to own a thing to count it
Only Café Q uses land, because the chapter treats land as always rented
Neither uses land, because the chapter reserves the word for forests and minerals alone

questions.q: A farmer gets advance weather updates on her phone, sows a week earlier and harvests more from the same field with the same family labour. Which description matches the chapter?
questions.a: Technology is acting as a facilitator, getting more output from the same inputs
o: Technology is acting as a facilitator, getting more output from the same inputs
The updates are land, because weather belongs with sunlight and air, which the chapter counts as land
The updates are labour, because reading and acting on them takes mental effort from her
The updates are entrepreneurship, because she chose to use them on her own farm

questions.q: Tarun says, 'A shop that only buys vegetables from a mandi and sells them is not an enterprise, because it produces nothing.' Judged by the chapter's definition, Tarun is
questions.a: wrong, because an enterprise may produce or sell goods or provide a service
o: wrong, because an enterprise may produce or sell goods or provide a service
right, because an enterprise has to produce goods from the inputs it combines
right, because only a factory can be called an enterprise by the chapter
wrong, because every enterprise must provide a service as well as sell goods

questions.q: Read the statements. (I) Every product around us goes through a production process before it reaches the user. (II) In economics, the four types of input are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
III only

questions.q: Assertion (A): Enterprises create opportunities for people to engage in economic activities. Reason (R): In economics, oil and natural gas are counted as land. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: A business that pays rent every month for the plot its shop stands on is paying to use ___.
questions.a: land

questions.q: Which pairing of an item with its factor of production is NOT correct according to the chapter?
questions.a: Sunlight and air: capital
o: Sunlight and air: capital
Forests and soil: land
Minerals and water: land
Oil, natural gas and water: land

questions.q: In Latha's group's report, mobile repair shops list 'tools, spare parts, knowledge and skills to handle mobile components', and vegetable vendors list 'fresh produce, baskets, weighing scale, cart or stall'. (a) Which input in the repair shops' row is not a physical thing, and under which factor of production does the chapter place that kind of input? (b) Which input in the vendors' row is a human-made durable asset, and so counts as capital?
questions.a: (a) The knowledge and skills are not a physical thing; they come from the people who do the repair, so they belong to labour, the physical and mental effort used in production. (b) The weighing scale, or the cart or stall, is a human-made durable asset used to produce goods and services, so it is capital.
s: (a) Names knowledge and skills and places them under labour
(b) Names the scale, cart or stall as capital

questions.q: True or False? 'In economics, technology is the fourth type of input, after land, labour and capital.' Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The four types are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship; technology is a facilitator that lets enterprises produce more with the same or fewer inputs.
s: Gives the verdict: false
Corrects it: the fourth type is entrepreneurship, and technology is a facilitator

questions.q: A garment unit opens in a town. (a) Name the factor of production that its rented plot belongs to. (b) Using the chapter, say what the unit does for the townspeople beyond making garments.
questions.a: (a) The rented plot is land, which a business may pay rent to use. (b) By combining inputs to create goods, an enterprise also generates opportunities for people to engage in economic activities, such as taking up jobs in the unit.
s: (a) Identifies the plot as land obtained on rent
(b) States that the enterprise generates opportunities for people to engage in economic activities

questions.q: Aarav says, 'The notebook I buy at the shop simply appears there; production is something that happens only inside factories.' (a) Which sentence of the chapter's opening contradicts him? (b) What name does the chapter give to the resources used in that process?
questions.a: (a) The chapter says every product around us goes through a production process before it finally reaches us, so the notebook did too. (b) The resources or inputs used in producing goods and services are called the factors of production.
s: (a) States that every product goes through a production process before it reaches the user
(b) Names the factors of production

questions.q: Latha's group lists salons and mobile repair shops among the enterprises of the locality, though neither makes a product on a shelf. Which words of the chapter's definition cover them, and what does that show about the definition?
questions.a: The definition says an enterprise 'produces or sells goods or provides a service', and salons and mobile repair shops provide a service. The definition is therefore wide: it covers shops, firms and factories whether they make goods, sell them or serve customers.
s: Cites 'provides a service' from the definition as covering both shops
Concludes that the definition covers makers, sellers and service providers alike

questions.q: Kabir says, 'At Pause Point the seven staff are labour and the stove and furniture are capital, but the rent Ratna pays is not connected to any factor of production.' Test his claim and say whether it is right, wrong or partly right.
questions.a: Partly right. The staff are labour, which is the physical and mental effort used in production, and the stove and furniture are human-made resources, so they are capital. But the rent is the payment for using land, and the chapter says businesses either purchase the land they need or pay rent to use it for a period of time, so it is connected to the factor land.
s: Accepts staff as labour and the stove and furniture as capital
Corrects the rent: it is paid to use land
Gives the verdict partly right

questions.q: A pavement tea stall needs only a pavement spot, water, a gas stove, a helper and the owner's own money. The owner says, 'I use no land at all.' Show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: The pavement spot is geographical land on which the stall stands, and the chapter's word 'land' also covers natural resources such as water. The stall uses both. So land is one of its inputs, whether the spot is owned or its use is paid for, and the owner's claim cannot hold.
s: Names the pavement spot as geographical land
Names water as a natural resource counted as land
Concludes that the stall uses land and the claim fails

questions.q: A business has these inputs: a rented plot, three workers, a loan of Rs 2 lakh and an owner who risked her savings on the idea. Write a short description of a business that could have exactly these inputs, and label each input with its factor.
questions.a: Sample: A small bakery run by Geeta. The rented plot is land, the three bakers are labour, the loan of Rs 2 lakh buys ovens and so is capital, and Geeta, who had the idea, risked her savings and decides how the bakery runs, is the entrepreneurship.
s: Describes a plausible business that matches the inputs
Labels plot as land, workers as labour and loan as capital
Labels the owner's idea and risk as entrepreneurship

questions.q: Ratna's cousin wants to open a roadside eatery like Pause Point. So far he has a plan, Rs 3 lakh of savings, and an offer of a plot on rent. Using the chapter, (a) say which of the four types of input he already has in hand and which he still must arrange, (b) name one natural resource, besides the plot itself, that the chapter counts in the same factor as his rented plot, and (c) explain why the chapter says an enterprise creates opportunities for others as well.
questions.a: (a) The plan and his readiness to risk his savings stand for entrepreneurship; the savings are capital; the plot on rent is land. Labour is what he still must arrange, by hiring staff, as Ratna did. (b) Water, or soil, air or sunlight, is a natural resource that the chapter counts as land, the same factor as his rented plot. (c) By combining land, labour and capital to create goods and services, an enterprise generates opportunities for people to engage in economic activities: the staff he hires earn a living and take part in the economy.
s: Identifies the entrepreneurship, capital and land he already has
Identifies labour as the input still to arrange
Names water or another natural resource as land
Explains that an enterprise generates opportunities for people

questions.q: A Class 8 class wants to run a one-day snack counter at the school fair. (a) List one input for each of the four types. (b) Name one facilitator the chapter mentions that could help them serve more with the same inputs. (c) The stoves, utensils and ingredients will cost Rs 12,000 (illustrative), and the class fund holds Rs 3,000. Which of the four types is short, and by how much?
questions.a: Sample: (a) Land: the corner of the playground they are allotted, and water; labour: the students who cook and serve; capital: the class fund, stoves and utensils; entrepreneurship: the student who comes up with the idea, takes the risk and decides. (b) Technology, such as paying through UPI at the click of a button, which lets the same students serve more customers. (c) Capital is short, by 12,000 - 3,000 = Rs 9,000, which the class would first seek from savings, family and friends.
s: Gives one correct input for each of the four types
Names a facilitator and links it to more output from the same inputs
Names capital as the short type
Computes the shortfall of Rs 9,000

questions.q:
Four Class 8 students surveyed 27 shops on one street (the figures are illustrative): 6 photocopy shops, 9 tea stalls, 5 cycle-repair shops and 7 tailors. Their table lists inputs, and under it they wrote three follow-up questions: (1) Where do the owners get the money they need? (2) Who taught the repairers their trade? (3) What made the owners start their business? They also wrote the note: 'Only tea stalls use land.'
(a) Point out the error in the note, with the chapter's reason.
(b) Which of the four types of input does question (3) point to, and which does question (1) point to?
(c) What share of the shops are tea stalls, to one decimal place?
(d) Predict: if three more tea stalls open, will the tea stalls' share rise or fall, and what will it be?
questions.a: (a) Every shop stands on ground it owns or pays rent for, and land in economics also includes resources such as water, so every shop type uses land. (b) Question (3) points to entrepreneurship, the idea and the risk; question (1) points to capital, the money. (c) 9/27 x 100 = 33.3 per cent. (d) With 12 tea stalls out of 30 shops the share rises to 12/30 x 100 = 40.0 per cent.
s: Corrects the note: every shop uses land, with the chapter's reason
Names entrepreneurship for question 3 and capital for question 1
Works out 33.3 per cent
Predicts a rise to 40.0 per cent

questions.q:
Kavita runs Masala Mill in a small town (the figures are illustrative). She rents a plot, owns a grinding machine, employs 8 workers and runs the mill herself, having borrowed to begin. The mill grinds 400 kg a day. A bulk order needs 500 kg a day. A new attachment would raise the mill's output by 30 per cent with the same 8 workers; it costs Rs 1.5 lakh. Kavita has Rs 90,000 in savings and her family can give Rs 30,000.
(a) Name the factor of production for each of: the rented plot, the machine, the 8 workers and Kavita herself.
(b) How much more money does she need for the attachment, and which source does the chapter name for a shortfall?
(c) How many kg a day would the mill grind with the attachment?
(d) She cannot meet the order with the present machine. Should she buy the attachment? Decide and justify with the figures.
questions.a: (a) The plot is land, the machine is capital, the 8 workers are labour and Kavita is the entrepreneur. (b) 1,50,000 - 90,000 - 30,000 = Rs 30,000, which she can get as a loan from a bank to meet the shortfall. (c) 400 x 1.30 = 520 kg a day. (d) Yes: 520 kg a day meets the 500 kg order with the same workers, the present 400 kg does not, and the Rs 30,000 gap can be met by a bank loan.
s: Classifies all four inputs correctly
Computes Rs 30,000 and names a bank loan
Computes 520 kg
Decides to buy, because 520 kg meets the 500 kg order and 400 kg does not

questions.q:
Two towns each have 5,000 factory workers who all put in 40 hours a week (the figures are illustrative). In Town A every worker has completed a skills course; its factories produce goods worth Rs 60 crore in the week. In Town B no worker has had any training; its factories produce goods worth Rs 35 crore in the week.
(a) Which input, rather than the effort supplied, would explain the difference? Give the chapter's reason.
(b) How many worker-hours does each town supply in the week?
(c) Work out the value of goods per worker-hour in each town.
(d) Predict Town B's weekly output if training raised its value per worker-hour to Town A's, with the same hours.
questions.a: (a) Human capital: the effort supplied is equal, but human capital is the quality and efficiency of labour, built on specialised skills, knowledge and expertise. (b) 5,000 x 40 = 2,00,000 worker-hours in each town. (c) Town A: 60 crore / 2,00,000 = Rs 3,000 per hour; Town B: 35 crore / 2,00,000 = Rs 1,750 per hour. (d) 2,00,000 x 3,000 = Rs 60 crore, the same as Town A.
s: Names human capital with the chapter's reason
Computes 2,00,000 worker-hours
Computes Rs 3,000 and Rs 1,750
Predicts Rs 60 crore

questions.q:
A student answered 'Why are human beings called a resource in production?' in three sentences. (1) 'Human beings are a resource only because they supply muscle power.' (2) 'A police officer or a scientist is therefore not part of labour, as their work is mental.' (3) 'Human capital is another name for the number of workers a business hires.'
(a) Correct sentence (1) using the chapter.
(b) Correct sentence (2) using the chapter.
(c) Correct sentence (3) using the chapter.
(d) Which of the three errors, if believed, would lead a factory owner to think that the only way to raise his firm's human capital is to hire more people? Name it and explain.
questions.a: (a) Human beings are a resource because they apply their knowledge, skills and decision-making abilities to create goods and services, not just muscle power. (b) Labour is physical and mental effort, so police officers and scientists supply labour too. (c) Human capital is the specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise required to perform labour, the quality and efficiency of it, not the head-count. (d) Sentence (3): if human capital meant the number of workers, adding workers would be the only way to add to it, whereas the chapter says it is the quality and efficiency of the labour.
s: Corrects (1): knowledge, skills and decision-making abilities
Corrects (2): labour is physical and mental effort
Corrects (3): human capital is skills, knowledge and expertise, not the number of workers
Names sentence (3), with the reason that head-count would make hiring the only route

questions.q: Two drivers of a city bus company work the same eight-hour shift on the same route in the same type of bus. The experienced driver completes more trips safely. Which input best explains the difference?
questions.a: Human capital: his skill and expertise make the same effort more efficient
o: Human capital: his skill and expertise make the same effort more efficient
Labour: only the experienced driver puts effort into the shift
Land: the experienced driver has a better claim on the road they both drive on
Capital: the experienced driver is using a better and newer bus than the other driver

questions.q: At Pause Point the chef develops a new recipe while a helper washes the utensils. Which statement is consistent with the chapter?
questions.a: Both supply labour, but the chef's role needs a different, specialised set of skills
o: Both supply labour, but the chef's role needs a different, specialised set of skills
Only the chef is a resource, since only inventing roles apply knowledge
Only the helper supplies labour, because labour means physical effort and nothing else
Both have the same human capital, since each is paid to work in the same kitchen every day

questions.q: Ravi repairs phones. Which of the following is a skill in the chapter's sense?
questions.a: His ability to fix a fault quickly, gained through practice and training
o: His ability to fix a fault quickly, gained through practice and training
His habit of opening the shop each morning at nine, which he has kept for years
The screwdrivers, testers and spare parts he keeps in the shop for repair work
His wish to open a second shop in the next town once his savings allow

questions.q: After reading that carpenters, farmers, construction workers, teachers and doctors all appear in the chapter, a student concludes, 'Only teachers and doctors use knowledge and skill; the others use only strength.' The chapter says
questions.a: all five use physical strength, knowledge and skill, in varying levels
o: all five use physical strength, knowledge and skill, in varying levels
the student is right, since farming and carpentry need no training
the student is right, because only mental work needs any training or skill
none of the five uses any knowledge, because labour is only physical effort

questions.q: Read the statements. (I) A skill is the ability to do an activity or job well without any practice or training. (II) The word labour refers to the physical and mental effort used in production. (III) Human capital refers to the specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise required to perform labour. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
III only

questions.q: Assertion (A): The chapter calls human beings a resource in production. Reason (R): Human beings apply their knowledge, skills and decision-making abilities to create goods and services. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: Which statement about people in production is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Only roles that need long study require dedication to do the job well
o: Only roles that need long study require dedication to do the job well
A scientist invents new technologies by applying knowledge and skills
A chef develops new recipes by applying decision-making abilities and skills
Every one of these roles needs its own special set of knowledge and skills

questions.q: Carpenters, farmers, construction workers, teachers and doctors all supply ___, though they use physical strength, knowledge and skill in different amounts.
questions.a: labour

questions.q: A police officer decides which of two roads to close after an accident. (a) Which of the three things human beings apply in production, according to the chapter, is she mainly using? (b) The chapter says every such role needs one more thing for the work to be done well. Name it.
questions.a: (a) Her decision-making abilities, which the chapter lists along with knowledge and skills. (b) Dedication: the chapter says they must all be dedicated to their work to do a good job.
s: (a) Names decision-making abilities
(b) Names dedication

questions.q: True or False? 'A teacher, a farmer and a doctor all supply labour, though each uses physical strength, knowledge and skill in a different amount.' Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says labour involves physical and mental effort, that carpenters, farmers, construction workers, teachers and doctors use varying levels of physical strength, knowledge and skill, and that everyone contributes differently.
s: Gives the verdict: true
Reason: all supply labour, with strength, knowledge and skill in varying levels

questions.q: A software developer sits at a desk all day and lifts nothing heavier than a laptop. (a) Does she supply labour, according to the chapter? (b) Which words of the chapter's statement on labour settle this?
questions.a: (a) Yes, she supplies labour. (b) The chapter says labour involves physical and mental effort used in production, so mental effort counts too; its own photographs show a software developer among those who work.
s: (a) Answers yes
(b) Cites physical and mental effort

questions.q: Raju is strong and works long hours but has never practised carpentry. Sheela works fewer hours but has trained in carpentry for two years. Using the chapter's definition of skill, who has the skill, and what does Raju's work still count as?
questions.a: Sheela has the skill, because a skill is the ability to do an activity or job well with practice and training, and she has both. Raju's work still counts as labour, since the physical and mental effort he puts in is part of production.
s: Names Sheela, using practice and training from the definition
States that Raju's effort still counts as labour

questions.q: The chapter says 'everyone contributes differently' and not 'everyone contributes equally'. Using a carpenter and a doctor, explain what the difference in the two statements means.
questions.a: A carpenter and a doctor use varying levels of physical strength, knowledge and skill, so what each puts into production differs. The chapter still counts both as contributing, helping create goods and services for society's needs; 'differently' describes the mix of effort and skill, not a ranking.
s: States that they use different levels of strength, knowledge and skill
States that both still contribute to society's needs

questions.q: Hari says, 'Human capital is only another word for labour, so a town with more workers must have more human capital.' Test his claim and give a verdict.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. Labour is the physical and mental effort used in production, whereas human capital is the specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise needed to perform that labour, meaning the quality and efficiency of labour and not its amount. A town can have many workers with little training and so little human capital.
s: Defines the two terms separately
Shows that quantity of workers does not decide quality and efficiency
Gives the verdict no

questions.q: A student says, 'A street sweeper's work does not count as labour because it needs more strength than knowledge.' Show that this cannot be right, using the chapter's definition.
questions.a: The chapter defines labour as the physical and mental effort used in production and says carpenters, farmers, construction workers and others use physical strength, knowledge and skill in varying levels. So a job that uses more strength and less knowledge is still labour, and everyone contributes differently, helping create goods and services for society's needs.
s: Cites labour as physical and mental effort
Cites the varying levels of strength, knowledge and skill
Concludes that the sweeper's work is labour

questions.q: Write a short account of a person who builds a skill, showing the practice and training she goes through and what she can do afterwards, using the chapter's definition of skill.
questions.a: Sample: Farida joins a tailoring class and practises every evening for a year. With practice and training she can cut and stitch a shirt well, which is a skill: the ability to do an activity or job well with practice and training.
s: Describes a person who practises
Shows training in the account
Ends with the ability to do the job well, as the definition says

questions.q: The chapter lists carpenters, farmers, construction workers, teachers and doctors together. Analyse why it puts such different jobs in one list.
questions.a: These jobs differ in how much physical strength, knowledge and skill they use, but the chapter says all use them in varying levels. Labour is the physical and mental effort used in production, so every one of them supplies it. Everyone contributes differently through their work, helping to create goods and services for society's needs, so the list shows that labour is not limited to muscle power.
s: States that the jobs use strength, knowledge and skill in varying levels
Links this to labour as physical and mental effort
Concludes that all contribute differently to society's needs

questions.q: Pause Point's staff (illustrative) include a cook, a cashier and a cleaner. Using the chapter, (a) say what each person applies in the work, (b) say what each role needs besides knowledge and skills, and (c) explain what it means that everyone contributes differently.
questions.a: (a) The cook applies knowledge and skills to develop dishes and decisions about the menu; the cashier applies knowledge of accounts and skill in handling money; the cleaner applies skill and effort in keeping the place fit to serve. (b) The chapter says each role needs its own special set of knowledge and skills and dedication to the work. (c) The three put in different amounts of physical strength, knowledge and skill, yet each helps create the goods and services for the customers.
s: States what the cook, cashier and cleaner each apply
States that each role needs its own set of knowledge and skills
States dedication to the work
Explains that everyone contributes differently

questions.q: The chapter says a police officer, a scientist and a chef 'must all be dedicated to their work to do a good job'. Justify whether dedication matters as much as knowledge and skill for such roles, using the chapter and the example of one of the three.
questions.a: The chapter names dedication as a requirement alongside a special set of knowledge and skills: 'of course, they all must be dedicated to their work to do a good job'. A chef who has the knowledge of recipes and the skill of cooking but is not dedicated would not develop new recipes, which is the contribution the chapter attributes to the role. A scientist's inventing of new technologies, likewise, depends on staying with the work. So dedication is a condition for the knowledge and skills to be put to use, and matters alongside them.
s: States that the chapter lists dedication with knowledge and skills
Uses one role as the example
Explains that without dedication the knowledge and skill are not put to use
Compares it with knowledge and skill
Reaches a clear justification

questions.q: Read the statements. (I) Training is the process of learning the skills required to do a particular job or activity. (II) Healthy workers can do more in shorter time periods. (III) The Economic Survey of India 2024 found that 65 per cent of people in India are above the age of 35. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only
o: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
III only

questions.q: A survey in a town reports an adult literacy rate of 72 per cent. Using the chapter's definition, this means that
questions.a: 72 of every 100 people aged 15 and above can read and write a simple statement with understanding
o: 72 of every 100 people aged 15 and above can read and write a simple statement with understanding
72 of every 100 people of all ages have completed Grade 8 and can pass an examination in any subject
72 of every 100 adults can read any book in any language they come across, with full understanding
72 of every 100 children aged 6 to 14 attend school regularly and can read a simple statement

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit the chapter links to healthy workers?
questions.a: They no longer need training to improve their skills
o: They no longer need training to improve their skills
They can do more in shorter time periods
They are able to be creative at work
They do not have to be away from work due to ill health

questions.q:
Match each situation with the idea it illustrates.
1. A firm holds a weekly 'one small improvement' meeting.
2. An apprentice learns safety rules and tool use by working on a site for months.
3. A child recovers from illness, returns to school and keeps up with the class.
4. Most of a country's people are young and working, and fewer depend on them.
(a) Training
(b) Kaizen
(c) Healthcare supporting cognitive development
(d) Demographic dividend
At a night class, a woman learns to read and write. A scooter mechanic's apprentice learns to find faults by working beside the mechanic for six months. Which pairing matches the chapter?
questions.a: Night class: education; apprenticeship: training
o: Night class: education; apprenticeship: training
Night class: training; apprenticeship: education
Both are education, because both teach something
Both are training, because both are for a livelihood

questions.q: (a) The workers of a workshop are always punctual, check every detail and take pride in the quality of what they make. Which work ethic described in the chapter does this match? (b) The chapter says such qualities of human capital contributed to what for that country?
questions.a: (a) The German work ethic, which places a high value on punctuality, attention to detail and quality. (b) They contributed to Germany's rise as a global leader in technology and manufacturing.
s: (a) Names the German work ethic
(b) States the rise as a global leader in technology and manufacturing

questions.q: A garment factory in Tiruppur starts a weekly meeting where each team suggests one small change in how work is done, and adopts the best. This resembles which idea in the chapter?
questions.a: Kaizen, meaning continuous improvement
o: Kaizen, meaning continuous improvement
The German work ethic of punctuality and quality
A demographic dividend from a young workforce
The adult literacy rate of the country

questions.q: (a) What does 'cognitive' refer to in the chapter? (b) Using (a), explain how a child who is often absent through illness is affected.
questions.a: (a) Cognitive refers to the process of learning, knowing and understanding. (b) Good health supports cognitive development and lets children attend school regularly and learn better, so a child often absent through illness loses school days and learns less well.
s: (a) States the meaning of cognitive
(b) Links ill health to missed school and weaker learning

questions.q:
A newspaper reports: 'India's adult literacy rate in 2023 was 85 per cent for males and 70 per cent for females (World Bank estimates).' A reader writes, 'So 15 per cent of Indian women cannot read.' Another says, 'With 30 per cent of women unable to read, India cannot gain a demographic dividend from its young population.'
(a) What does the chapter's adult literacy rate count?
(b) What error does the first reader make, and what is the correct share of adult women who are not literate?
(c) In a town of 600 adult women who match the national rate, how many are not literate?
(d) Judge the second reader's claim using the chapter's statement about when the dividend is realised.
questions.a: (a) The percentage of people aged 15 and above who can read and write with understanding a short, simple statement about their everyday life. (b) The reader mistakes the 15-point gap between the male and female rates for the share of women who are not literate; the correct share is 100 - 70 = 30 per cent. (c) 30 per cent of 600 = 180 women. (d) The claim goes beyond the chapter: it says the 65 per cent of people below 35 give the possibility of a dividend, which is realised only if individuals have access to quality education, health, training and skilling, so literacy figures alone do not show that India cannot gain it.
s: States the definition with age 15 and above
Identifies the confusion of gap with share and gives 30 per cent
Computes 180
Judges the claim as not supported, using the conditions for the dividend

questions.q: The chapter's closing summary says human capital is influenced by education, training, health, use of technology and social context, while the body of the chapter has three headings of facilitators. questions.a: Relying on far-off sources instead of local inputs can halt production in a disruption
o: Relying on far-off sources instead of local inputs can halt production in a disruption
Capital-intensive production needs no labour at all, so it is unaffected by shipments
New techniques such as 3-D printing revive dying art forms by producing handloom goods at scale
Human effort runs through every stage of production, so stopping one stage changes nothing else

questions.q: A farm buys a harvesting machine and now needs 4 workers where it earlier needed 20. The chapter's account of this is that
questions.a: new techniques can change the proportion of factors used, lowering dependence on labour
o: new techniques can change the proportion of factors used, lowering dependence on labour
labour has stopped being a factor of production on that farm, since machines now do the work of people
the factors are no longer interconnected, since one of them was cut back so sharply on the farm
the farm's output must have fallen, because fewer people are working in its fields now

questions.q: A student says, 'Every input for a mobile phone factory has to come from within one city.' Which statement from the chapter's account of geographic interconnectedness answers her?
questions.a: Inputs are available at different locations, and enterprises can procure and combine them
o: Inputs are available at different locations, and enterprises can procure and combine them
Inputs must be bought from far-off places, since local inputs are never available to enterprises
Enterprises must produce each input themselves before combining it with the others
Inputs are the same in every place, so the location of the factory does not matter

questions.q: Read the statements. (I) The factors of production complement each other and are interconnected. (II) Output from agriculture, construction and handicrafts is capital-intensive, while semiconductor chips and satellites are labour-intensive. (III) A supply chain is a network of individuals, organisations, resources, activities and technology involved in the production and sale of goods. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
III only

questions.q: Assertion (A): The chapter calls the making of semiconductor chips labour-intensive. Reason (R): Semiconductor chips and satellites require more capital and specialised machinery. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, R is true
o: A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false

questions.q: The chapter calls the output of the agriculture, construction and handicraft sectors ___-intensive.
questions.a: labour

questions.q: Which of these statements about supply chains and inputs is NOT supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Relying on local inputs instead of far-off sources is what caused the COVID-19 halt
o: Relying on local inputs instead of far-off sources is what caused the COVID-19 halt
Enterprises can procure inputs from varied locations and combine them to produce goods
A disruption in the supply chain can result in a halt in the production process
Missing or misused factors can make production inefficient or even halt it altogether

questions.q: A weaving cooperative uses 3-D printing to make handloom products on a large scale to serve the market. Which statement from the chapter fits?
questions.a: 3-D printing can help revive dying textile art forms by producing handloom products at scale
o: 3-D printing can help revive dying textile art forms by producing handloom products at scale
3-D printing has made textile art forms capital-intensive by definition, so no labour is needed
3-D printing shows that new techniques never change the proportion of the factors used
3-D printing is a factor that has replaced land, labour and capital in textiles

questions.q: Faisal says, 'Satellites are capital-intensive, so no labour is needed to make them.' Test his claim and give a verdict.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. Capital-intensive means the product requires more capital and specialised machinery, not no labour. The chapter also says human effort is involved at every stage of production, with teams of engineers and project managers using their expertise, and that the factors complement each other.
s: Explains that capital-intensive means more capital, not no labour
Cites human effort at every stage
Gives the verdict no

questions.q: Show that a mobile phone factory could not run on capital, meaning money and machinery, alone.
questions.a: The chapter says human effort is involved at every stage of production to design, supervise and improve products and processes, with engineers and project managers using their expertise. It also says the entrepreneur guides how resources are used, and that land and factory space must be procured. Since the factors complement each other, money and machines without land and people cannot make phones.
s: States that human effort is needed at every stage
States the need for land and the entrepreneur's guidance
Concludes that the factors complement each other so capital alone fails

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a new technique changes the proportion of the factors a business uses. State which factor's share falls and which rises.
questions.a: Sample: A cloth merchant in Surat buys machines that weave in an hour what ten workers wove in a day. His dependence on labour falls and his use of capital and machinery rises, as the chapter says increased machine use can lower dependence on labour.
s: Describes a plausible new technique in a business
States which factor falls
States which rises, with the chapter's link

questions.q: The chapter says geographic interconnectedness gives businesses access to varied inputs, and also that relying on far-off sources can halt production. State one advantage and one risk of sourcing inputs from far away, and say what the chapter contrasts far-off sources with.
questions.a: The advantage is access to varied inputs from many places that enterprises can combine. The risk is that a disruption in the supply chain, as in COVID-19, can result in a halt in production. The chapter contrasts far-off sources with local inputs, so using local inputs for part of the supply reduces the risk.
s: States the advantage of access to varied inputs
States the risk of a halt in production
Names local inputs as the contrast

questions.q: A factory has money and machines but no skilled workers. (a) What does the chapter say can happen when a factor is missing? (b) Which statement about the factors explains why money and machines cannot make up for the gap?
questions.a: (a) Production can become inefficient or be halted. (b) The factors complement each other and are interconnected, so each is needed with the others.
s: (a) States inefficient or halted production
(b) States that the factors complement each other and are interconnected

questions.q: True or False? 'A business can combine inputs drawn from different geographic locations to produce a single good.' Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says production inputs are available at different geographic locations and enterprises can procure them from these varied locations and combine them.
s: Gives the verdict: true
Reason: inputs lie in different places and enterprises procure and combine them

questions.q: The chapter says all the inputs are 'working like puzzle pieces'. Explain the comparison, using one input whose absence would halt production.
questions.a: Like puzzle pieces, each input is needed together with the others to make the whole, which is the goods and services we rely on. If one piece is missing, such as the financial resources to procure land, factory space, machinery and skilled workers, production can become inefficient or be halted.
s: Explains that the inputs fit together and each is needed
Gives an example of a missing input halting production

questions.q: Unit P weaves mats by hand with 30 workers and two looms (treat hand-weaving as a handicraft). Unit Q makes semiconductor chips with 30 workers and a great deal of specialised machinery. (a) Which unit does the chapter's account make more labour-intensive? (b) What does the chapter say Unit Q's kind of output requires more of?
questions.a: (a) Unit P, since handicraft output relies more on labour. (b) More capital and specialised machinery, which is why semiconductor chips are capital-intensive.
s: (a) Names Unit P
(b) Names capital and specialised machinery

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say is needed to procure land, factory space, machinery and skilled workers for a phone factory? (b) Which of the four types of input does this show to be linked with all the others?
questions.a: (a) Financial resources. (b) Capital, which is needed to obtain land, machinery and workers, so the factors are interconnected.
s: (a) Names financial resources
(b) Names capital as linked to the others

questions.q: A tannery cluster gives work to two thousand families in a town but releases untreated waste into the nearby river. Which statement matches the chapter's account?
questions.a: The cluster helps the local economy, but its waste can pollute rivers and soil; it must use resources responsibly
o: The cluster helps the local economy, but its waste can pollute rivers and soil; it must use resources responsibly
The jobs it gives outweigh the pollution, so the cluster owes nothing to the river or to the people living on its banks
The pollution is dangerous only to people, and not to the animals and plants that live along the river and soil
Only the government, and not the producer, is responsible for keeping the river clean and its water safe

questions.q: A phone-repair shop has 50 old phones and may either send them for recycling or bury them behind the shop. According to the chapter, why does burying them matter?
questions.a: Lead and mercury can leak into the ground and water, which endangers people, animals and plants
o: Lead and mercury can leak into the ground and water, which endangers people, animals and plants
The shop loses the value of the capital that the phones represent, which harms the shop alone and nobody else
The phones give off waste that harms only the shop's own workers, and only while they stay in the shop
Old phones cannot be recycled at all, so burying them is the only way to dispose of them safely

questions.q: A factory pays its workers fairly, but never trains them, and denies them the paid leave that the rules provide. Which two responsibilities from the chapter is it neglecting?
questions.a: Skill development and training, and workplace rights and protections
o: Skill development and training, and workplace rights and protections
Fair pay and working conditions, and skill development and training
Fair compensation and working conditions, and workplace rights and protections
Corporate Social Responsibility, and fair compensation and working conditions

questions.q: Which action of a paper mill best fits the chapter's idea of meeting today's needs without making it harder for future generations to meet theirs?
questions.a: It plants new trees to replace those it uses and recycles its wastewater
o: It plants new trees to replace those it uses and recycles its wastewater
It draws more river water now, as later generations will find another source
It switches off its pollution controls for a year to cut costs
It sells part of its land so as to expand production quickly

questions.q: Read the statements. (I) Natural resources are limited and cannot be degraded. (II) Workplace rights and protections include preventing discrimination and providing benefits like health care or paid leave. (III) Corporate Social Responsibility includes reducing polluting activities and treating employees and customers with respect. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
III only

questions.q: Assertion (A): India was the first nation in the world to bring a Corporate Social Responsibility law, in 2014. Reason (R): Waste from Tamil Nadu's leather factories can pollute rivers and soil. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q:
Match each action of a firm with the responsibility the chapter names for it.
1. It funds a course so that its staff stay competitive in the labour market.
2. It pays for cleaning a lake near its plant and for health camps in nearby villages.
3. It pays wages on time at a fair rate and keeps its machines safely guarded.
4. It gives paid leave and takes steps to prevent discrimination.
(a) Fair compensation and working conditions
(b) Skill development and training
(c) Workplace rights and protections
(d) Corporate Social Responsibility
Under India's 2014 CSR law, a company whose average profit over its last three years is Rs 15 crore (an illustrative figure) must spend Rs ___ lakh on CSR activities.

Lakshmi Tanneries made profits of Rs 9 crore, Rs 12 crore and Rs 15 crore in its last three years (the figures are illustrative). Its annual note claims, 'We have met our legal duty on CSR by spending Rs 18 lakh on cleaning the town lake.'
(a) What does the chapter say India's CSR law of 2014 required of companies?
(b) What is the average profit of the last three years?
(c) How much did the law require this company to spend?
(d) Judge the company's claim, and say how much more it would have to spend to meet the law.
questions.a: (a) It mandated companies to spend 2 per cent of their average profits of the last three years on CSR activities. (b) (9 + 12 + 15) / 3 = Rs 12 crore. (c) 2 per cent of Rs 12 crore = Rs 24 lakh. (d) The claim is not supported: Rs 18 lakh is less than Rs 24 lakh, so it would have to spend 24 - 18 = Rs 6 lakh more.
s: States 2 per cent of average profits of the last three years
Computes Rs 12 crore
Computes Rs 24 lakh
Judges the claim unsupported and gives Rs 6 lakh more

questions.q:
A phone-repair shop in Indore collects 200 old phones a year (the figures are illustrative). Each year it sends 60 to a recycler and puts the rest in a pit behind the shop. The owner offers two fixes: (X) send all phones from now on to a recycler, or (Y) put a fence round the pit and keep filling it.
(a) How many phones went into the pit this year, and how many would be in it after two years at this rate?
(b) Which two harmful substances can leak from phones that are not recycled properly, and where can they go?
(c) Whom does the chapter say the pollution can endanger?
(d) Which fix addresses the danger the chapter describes, and why?
questions.a: (a) 200 - 60 = 140 phones this year; 140 x 2 = 280 after two years. (b) Lead and mercury, which can leak into the ground and water. (c) People, animals and plants. (d) X: the chapter's danger is leaking into ground and water, which a fence does not stop, whereas recycling the phones removes them from the pit.
s: Computes 140 and 280
Names lead and mercury and ground and water
Names people, animals and plants
Chooses X, because a fence does not stop the leaking into ground and water

questions.q: Dev says, 'The leather factories give people work, so their waste is not the producer's concern.' Test his claim and give a verdict.
questions.a: No, the claim is wrong. The chapter says the leather factories help the local economy, but their waste can pollute rivers and soil, which can be dangerous for people, animals and plants. It is therefore important for producers to use natural resources responsibly, whatever other good they do.
s: Accepts that the factories help the local economy
States that the waste can pollute rivers and soil
Gives the verdict no, with the producers' responsibility

questions.q: A firm pays its workers the legal wage and keeps its premises safe but offers no training. Show that it cannot claim to have met all three responsibilities the chapter names towards workers.
questions.a: The chapter names three responsibilities: fair compensation and working conditions, skill development and training, and workplace rights and protections. The firm meets the first through wages and safety. But skill development and training means investing in training and education so that workers develop the skills to remain competitive, and the firm offers none. So one responsibility is unmet.
s: Names the three responsibilities
Credits the firm with the first
Shows that the training responsibility is unmet

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a company's Corporate Social Responsibility activity addresses the well-being of a local community, and name the part of the chapter's description it matches.
questions.a: Sample: A cement company runs a free eye-care camp and builds a drinking-water tank for the villages around its plant. This matches the chapter's description of CSR as addressing the well-being of local communities, one of the things CSR includes along with reducing polluting activities and treating employees and customers with respect.
s: Describes a company activity benefiting a local community
Names the matching part: well-being of local communities
Links it to the meaning of CSR as addressing social and environmental concerns

questions.q: A paper mill cuts trees for its pulp. Using the chapter, explain why reducing waste alone may not be enough, and what else the chapter asks of producers.
questions.a: The chapter says natural resources are limited and can be degraded. Reducing waste and avoiding pollution save resources, but the trees are still used up. So the chapter also asks producers to adopt sustainable practices that replenish natural resources for future use, so that future generations can meet their needs.
s: States that resources are limited and can be degraded
States that reducing waste alone still leaves the trees used
Names practices that replenish resources for future use

questions.q: True or False? 'A dye unit that recycles its wastewater before releasing it into a water body is following the chapter's advice on sustainable practices.' Give the verdict, then the reason or the correction.
questions.a: True. The chapter says producers should reduce waste, avoid pollution and protect the environment, and its figures show industrial wastewater being recycled before release into water bodies as a sustainable practice.
s: Gives the verdict: true
Reason: the chapter asks producers to reduce waste and avoid pollution

questions.q: A furniture maker begins using recycled wood as an input. (a) Which of the chapter's practices for producers does this match? (b) Why does the chapter say such practices matter for natural resources?
questions.a: (a) Adopting sustainable practices and reducing waste, since recycled products are used as inputs. (b) Natural resources are limited and can be degraded if we are not careful, so they must be used so that future generations can still meet their needs.
s: (a) Names sustainable practices or reducing waste
(b) States that natural resources are limited and can be degraded

questions.q: (a) Name two things that Corporate Social Responsibility includes, according to the chapter. (b) A bakery gives free bread each week to a school nearby. Which of your two is it closest to?
questions.a: (a) Reducing polluting activities, addressing the well-being of local communities, and treating employees and customers with respect; any two. (b) Addressing the well-being of local communities.
s: (a) Names two things CSR includes
(b) Names the well-being of local communities

questions.q: A firm replaces workers with machines and lets them go without any retraining. (a) What does the chapter say the responsibility for skill development and training asks of employers? (b) Which responsibility is the firm neglecting?
questions.a: (a) To invest in training and education so that workers develop the skills necessary to remain competitive in the labour market. (b) Skill development and training.
s: (a) States investing in training and education so workers stay competitive
(b) Names skill development and training

questions.q: A stitching section has broken wiring and no fire exit, though wages are paid on time. (a) Which part of the first of the three responsibilities is being ignored? (b) What does the same responsibility say about pay?
questions.a: (a) Working conditions: workers must work in a safe environment. (b) Workers must be paid fairly for their labour.
s: (a) Names a safe working environment
(b) Names fair pay for their labour

questions.q: A tannery with 120 workers (an illustration) is considering four steps: (i) cutting its spending on worker safety, (ii) ending all training, (iii) letting its waste run into a river, (iv) spending its CSR money on a hoarding with its name. For each step, name the responsibility from the chapter that it would breach, and give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (i) Fair compensation and working conditions: workers must work in a safe environment. (ii) Skill development and training: employers must invest in training so workers stay competitive. (iii) Responsibility towards natural resources: waste can pollute rivers and soil, which is dangerous for people, animals and plants. (iv) Corporate Social Responsibility: it is meant to address social and environmental concerns, such as reducing polluting activities and the well-being of local communities, which a hoarding does not.
s: (i) Names safe working conditions
(ii) Names skill development and training
(iii) Names natural resources and the harm of pollution
(iv) Names CSR and its purpose
Gives a chapter reason for each, not only a label

questions.q: Justify the statement 'Responsibility is part of production, not an extra after it.' Use the chapter's points on natural resources, workers and Corporate Social Responsibility.
questions.a: Natural resources are limited and can be degraded if we are not careful, and production uses them, so producers must use them responsibly to meet today's needs without harming future generations. The chapter lists responsibilities towards workers, namely fair pay and safe conditions, training, and rights and protections, alongside those towards natural resources. CSR asks businesses to address social and environmental concerns, and India's law of 2014 made companies spend 2 per cent of average profits of the last three years on it. The chapter's closing point is that the resources must be preserved and used judiciously, so responsibility belongs inside production.
s: States that natural resources are limited and degradable, so used responsibly
States that the chapter lists responsibilities towards workers alongside those towards natural resources
States the CSR law of 2014 and its 2 per cent rule
Cites the chapter's closing point on preserving and using resources judiciously
Reaches a clear justification
